title: Big Tech Stock Prices
text:
This dataset contains daily stock prices and trading volume for 14 large tech companies from 2010 to 2023. The line plot below represents the adjusted closing prices for Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Amazon, household tech names with large market capitalizations (the stock prices for these four companies were recorded on 12/29/2022 at the latest). Adjusted closing price is the closing price adjusted for stock splits and dividends issued, so that stock prices can be accurately compared across the observed time frame.


Code
library(tidyverse)

big_tech_stock_prices <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-02-07/big_tech_stock_prices.csv')

big_tech_stock_prices |>
    filter(stock_symbol == "AAPL" | stock_symbol == "MSFT" | stock_symbol == "NVDA" | stock_symbol == "AMZN") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = adj_close, color = stock_symbol)) + 
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
    labs(x = "Date", y = "Adjusted close price (USD)", color = "Ticker", title = "Adjusted closing price, 2010 to 2022")









Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Amazon grew rapidly from 2010 to 2021, but fell sharply after their peaks in late 2021 to early 2022. Nvidia and Amazon lost more than half of their value, while Microsoft and Amazon lost a little less than a third of their value.
Data source: TidyTuesday, February 7, 2023.
Original data: Evan Gower compiled the data in 2023. The Big Tech Stock Prices data set comes from Yahoo Finance and was obtained through Kaggle.

title: NFL Attendance
text:
This dataset records weekly and season-total attendance for every NFL team from 2000 to 2019. The plot shows total league attendance by season.


Code
library(tidyverse)

attendance <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-02-04/attendance.csv')

attendance |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarize(league_total = sum(weekly_attendance, na.rm = TRUE) / 2) |> #The data set reports each game's weekly attendance twice, one time for each team that played, so the weekly total attendances are divided by two.
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = league_total / 1000000)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "Season", y = "Total attendance (millions)", title = "NFL total attendance by season, 2000 to 2019")









NFL total attendance was lowest in 2001, at about 16.3 million total attendees, but jumped sharply to a little less than 17 million total attendees in 2002. The attendance continued to grow until 2006, and then fell until 2010. It grew again after 2010 with the exception of the 2015 season, and peaked at about 17.79 million total attendees in 2016. Attendance fell after that, ending at just above 17 million people in 2019.
Data source: TidyTuesday, February 4, 2020.
Original data: The data comes from the Pro Football Reference website, published by Sports Reference LLC. Each individual year was obtained from each year’s NFL attendance page; see 2019’s attendance data here.

title: Shakespeare Dialogue
Room Draw Simulation
text:
The Pomona room draw is a random assignment of a time, starting at 5:00pm and running one slot every 3 minutes with 4 students per slot, and with each class registering on a different day, for students to select their place of residence for the next school year. This analysis focuses on rising seniors, as they are the first class to register and therefore have access to the nicest rooms. The question I hope to solve through this simulation is how the chances of getting a group time at or before 5:27pm (the time the last Sontag/Dialynas suite [a suite of 4] was selected in Fall 2025) change as group size goes from 1 to 8 (note there are no groups of 7 and students can group up with a friend and adopt the earliest time to get a better room). I plan on simulating multiple random room draws and estimating the probability of each group size achieving a time at or before 5:27pm, because working it out by hand is quite difficult.
The room_draw function produces one random sample of all seniors’ positions in the housing draw, takes the earliest position of the group of students (the random time the student is assigned if group size is 1), and checks whether the group time is 40 or lower (5:27pm is when the last Sontag/Dialynas suite of 4 was selected, and at 4 students every 3 minutes starting at 5, that leaves 40 students with times that give them a good room). The room_draw_simulation function repeats the room_draw function 10,000 times and calculates the share of successful group room draws. The first map_lgl runs the room_draw 10000 times, and the second map runs the room_draw_simulation for each possible student group (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8).


Code
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(47)

room_draw <- \(group_size) {
rand_students <- sample(1:325) #random sample of the class
student_group <- rand_students[1:group_size] #random times from sample for each student in a given group size
earliest_student <- min(student_group) #earliest student housing draw time out of the group
good_room <- earliest_student <= 40 #4 people per group, one group every 3 minutes. 10 groups up to 5:27, so the most sought-after rooms are taken by the first 40 students.
return(good_room)
}
room_draw_simulation <- \(group_size) {
 return(data.frame(
    group_size = group_size, 
    good_room_prob = mean(
        map_lgl(1:10000, \(i) room_draw(group_size))))) #runs the room_draw function with an inputted group_size 10000 times and finds the proportion of successful draws (mean of TRUE = 1 and FALSE = 0 gives proportion of TRUE)
}
possible_groups = c(1,2,3,4,5,6,8)
results <- list_rbind(map(possible_groups, room_draw_simulation)) #list_rbind stacks the rows into one per group size
results


  group_size good_room_prob
1          1         0.1241
2          2         0.2276
3          3         0.3303
4          4         0.4114
5          5         0.4857
6          6         0.5444
7          8         0.6553


The table above displays each potential group size, and the proportion of randomly sampled times that give a good room to the group. The columns are group size and good room probability, which is calculated as the average of the TRUE or FALSE values given if the earliest time in the group is less than or equal to 40. The students who choose not to group have about a 12% chance of getting a good room, while the group of 8 has roughly a 66% probability.


Code
ggplot(results, aes(x = group_size, y = good_room_prob)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Group Size vs. Probability of Drawing a Good Room", x = "Group size", y = "Probability of getting a good room")









This graph illustrates the relationship between group size and the probability of drawing a good room. The line rises from about 0.12 probability of getting a good room at group size of 1 to a probability of about 0.66 once the group reaches 8 students. Each additional student added to the group increases their likelihood of getting a good room, with the first two friends added increasing the probability by about 0.1. The gain per extra person added falls after that point (about 0.08, then 0.07, then 0.06, and about 0.06 per person from 6 to 8).
In this simulation, I ran the room draw on one class of 325 students, the number of seniors who selected housing in the Fall 2025 room draw; note that group size 7 is not included because the HRL website lists no room type for groups of that size. The probability that a randomly assigned time gives a student a good room rises from about a 0.12 probability to about a 0.66 probability as group size increases. Every member’s position in the group is random and independent, and the cutoff is the 40th position (the students whose earliest group times are from 5:00pm to 5:27pm); however, the model treats every group member as a senior in the same selection pool whereas, in reality, seniors can pull juniors and sophomores into their group. The numbers obtained are simulation estimates, with a small margin of error (about plus or minus 0.01 at 10,000 trials).
